title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Wind Turbines | PT (US)
description: Liquid penetrant testing of wind turbine castings, machined bores, stainless and aluminum parts, and weld repairs at US plants and sites. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Wind Turbines: Dye Penetrant Inspection of Hardware, Housings and Repairs
html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing (PT, or dye penetrant inspection) on wind turbine parts that cannot be examined by magnetic particle: aluminum and stainless hardware, machined bearing seats and bores, cast housings, and weld repairs on nonmagnetic or coated material. Technicians are mobilized to a fabrication plant, a repair shop or a turbine site in the United States for the agreed scope. Request a PT inspection quote with a list of parts, materials and drawings.

Where penetrant testing fits on a wind turbine

Most structural steel in a wind turbine is magnetic, and for that steel magnetic particle inspection is usually the first surface method; see magnetic particle inspection for wind turbines. Penetrant testing earns its place on everything else, and on surfaces where a magnetic field is awkward to apply. A turbine has plenty of that: stainless fasteners and fittings, aluminum covers and housings, brass and bronze bushings, copper conductors in the lightning protection path, and machined faces whose fine finish would be marred by a yoke or contact heads.

PT finds surface-breaking cracks by capillary action. A thin liquid with dye is applied to a cleaned surface and allowed to seep into any crack open to that surface; the excess is removed, a developer is applied, and the trapped liquid bleeds back to show the crack. It cannot see below the surface, cannot find a crack that has been smeared shut, and gives no information about wall thickness; for internal flaws in tower welds see ultrasonic testing for wind turbines. The method overview is on our penetrant testing page.

Machined bores, bearing seats and shaft journals

Bearing seats in gearbox and main bearing housings, and journals on shafts, are precision surfaces. Fatigue cracks and fretting damage occur at the edges of those surfaces, where load transfers from the bearing into the housing. Magnetizing these parts for MT can leave residual magnetism that attracts debris into a bearing, which owners want to avoid, and a finely machined face can hide indications under particles. Penetrant testing leaves the part unmagnetized, shows fine cracks on a smooth surface clearly, and can be cleaned off completely. For critical surfaces we use a fluorescent system under black light in a darkened enclosure, because it detects tighter cracks than visible dye does.

Where a part comes from the original equipment manufacturer, the manufacturer's inspection instruction takes precedence. We follow the document and state its revision in the report.

Cast housings, aluminum parts and stainless hardware

Gearbox housings, hub castings, frame castings and bearing carriers are often cast iron or cast steel. Ductile iron is magnetic, but its rough surface and casting skin can make MT unreliable and PT is chosen after machining. Aluminum nacelle structures and converter or transformer enclosures are never magnetic, and weld repairs on them are examined by PT. Stainless steel fasteners and fittings are common where corrosion is a concern, and those must be examined with penetrant products that are low in halogens and sulfur as required for austenitic alloys under ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165. We use batch-certified materials for that work and clean the part afterward. The job page on penetrant testing of castings describes the technique on cast surfaces in more detail.

Weld repairs and the lightning protection path

Repairs on nacelle frames, hub parts and tower attachments are examined by PT when the base metal or the weld deposit is nonmagnetic, or when the area is too confined for a yoke. A repair sequence typically examines the excavation before welding, then the finished weld after grinding. Lightning protection components include copper and aluminum conductors, brush assemblies and bonding straps; where a bonding lug or strap has been repaired, PT is a way of confirming that no surface crack remains in the lug. We do not test the electrical performance of the lightning system, which is a specialist task for the turbine maker.

Technique: penetrant, dwell and cold weather

Field work uses solvent-removable penetrant with a solvent cleaner and a nonaqueous developer, because it needs no water supply or wash station. The sequence is cleaning, applying penetrant, a dwell time set by the procedure, wiping the excess with dry then dampened cloth, thin developer coating and a developing time before evaluation. Cleaning is the foundation of reliable PT: oil, grease, paint and corrosion products fill cracks and block penetrant, so we use solvent and mechanical cleaning, and avoid shot blasting, which can peen cracks closed.

Temperature is the main wind site issue. ASME Section V Article 6 normally allows examination of surfaces between about 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Cold towers, shaded surfaces and winter outdoor work often fall below that, so the procedure must be qualified at the lower temperature, or the part must be warmed. Wet or frosty surfaces must be dry before penetrant goes on. Our explainer on Section V Article 6 sets out each step, and the MT versus PT comparison helps decide which method belongs on which part.

Reading indications: relevant, nonrelevant and false

A penetrant examination produces many marks, and the technician's job is to sort them. A crack gives a sharp, continuous or broken line that bleeds back after the developer dries. Porosity in a casting appears as scattered round dots. Machining marks, a rough weld surface and wiped-off residue can leave diffuse or streaked patterns that are not defects. Because a developer can hide a poorly wiped surface, we do not examine a part unless the cleaning step has been done to the procedure, and we repeat the examination from the start if the surface was wiped unevenly. Indications are recorded by location and size; nonrelevant ones are noted as such with a reason, so a reviewer can follow the call.

On a wind site, the same technician may examine a machined bore, a stainless fitting and a weld repair in one visit, so the report separates each by component and procedure. If a part fails, we mark the indication with a paint pen where the owner allows it and photograph it with a scale. The ASNT Level III reviews borderline calls before the report is released, and where the call affects a repair decision we raise it with the owner's engineer rather than leave it to a footnote.

Codes and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 govern the method. Acceptance criteria are not in those documents; they come from the turbine manufacturer, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, or the owner's specification for repairs. Typically linear indications above a stated length and rounded indications beyond size and spacing limits are rejected, and relevant indications from non-defect causes such as machining marks are evaluated and recorded. Our report names the specification and revision. If the documents conflict, we ask the owner or fabricator for written direction.

Who performs the work

PT is performed by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. We supply the examination record; owners, manufacturers and engineers decide on repair and service life.

What the report contains

  • Turbine, tower or part identification matched to your drawings
  • Procedure number and revision, and the governing specification
  • Penetrant, cleaner and developer type, with batch numbers and contaminant certifications where required
  • Surface preparation, dwell and developing times, and surface temperature
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication with location, size and accept or reject
  • Sketches or photographs and any coverage limit

What to send for a quote

  • Part list with quantities and drawings
  • Material for each part, including any dissimilar joints
  • Contaminant limits from your specification
  • Acceptance criteria and the document they come from
  • Surface condition, coatings and the working temperature
  • Location, access method, lighting and power
  • Schedule window, orientation or badging requirements and the address

What we do not do

We do not inspect composite blades. Radiography is not something Atlantis performs in the United States, since industrial radiography falls under NRC and Agreement State licensing. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not decide whether a part may stay in service; the owner, manufacturer or engineer does that.

Planning a wind turbine PT scope

PT takes longer per part than MT because of the dwell and developing time, so batch work is planned in stages: clean everything, apply penetrant to the first group, wipe and develop, and evaluate while the next group dwells. Parts exposed to rain or low temperature need protection. Inside a nacelle, bright lighting can wash out fluorescent indications, so the area is screened or the part is examined in a dark enclosure. The site arranges hoists, lifts and rope teams under its own safety plan; our technicians are mobilized for the scope and follow site orientation, lockout and badging requirements.

Where we work in the US for wind energy

  • Omaha: Plains wind projects and the shops that repair their parts.
  • Wichita: Kansas wind farms and machining suppliers, including aluminum work.
  • Oklahoma City: Oklahoma wind projects far from major repair shops.
  • Denver: Colorado and Wyoming wind farms in cold, high-altitude air.
  • Midland: West Texas wind and dust-heavy sites.
  • Tulsa: northeast Oklahoma fabrication and machining.
  • Minneapolis: upper Midwest sites where winter work dominates.
  • Spokane: Pacific Northwest wind and aluminum fabrication.

Training your own PT technicians

Repair shops and owner-operators who want in-house PT can start with PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and practice on the penetrant testing simulator. The manufacturing NDT training page covers fabrication needs. Since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, we can help with a written practice and a qualified procedure.

faq.q: When should wind turbine parts get penetrant testing instead of magnetic particle?
faq.a: When the part is nonmagnetic, such as aluminum, stainless or bronze, when a smooth machined surface should not be magnetized, or when a yoke cannot reach. For tower steel and bolts, MT is usually the better first choice.

faq.q: Can PT be done on a cold tower in winter?
faq.a: Only if the procedure is qualified for the surface temperature. The standard range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, so colder parts need a qualified low-temperature procedure or must be warmed. Wet or frosty surfaces must be dry first.

faq.q: Why do stainless fasteners need special penetrant materials?
faq.a: Halogens and sulfur left on austenitic stainless steel or nickel alloys can promote cracking. ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 limit them, so we use batch-certified products and clean the part afterward.

faq.q: Can you examine bearing seats without leaving magnetism?
faq.a: Yes. PT leaves no residual magnetism, so it suits precision bearing seats and journals. For critical surfaces we use fluorescent penetrant under black light in a darkened area to find tight cracks.

faq.q: Who decides if a penetrant indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The manufacturer's instruction, AWS D1.1 or the owner's specification supplies the criteria, and the report names it. Atlantis evaluates against those criteria; the owner or engineer decides on repair.
No. Blades are composite and need other inspection methods that Atlantis does not offer. We inspect metal parts: castings, housings, hardware, shafts and weld repairs.

faq.q: What do you need to quote PT on wind turbine parts?
faq.a: A part list and drawings, materials and any contaminant limits, acceptance criteria, surface condition and temperature, access and lighting, schedule window, site address and any badging or orientation requirements.

faq.q: Does PT find cracks under paint?
faq.a: Not reliably. Penetrant must enter the crack, so paint, oil and corrosion must be removed first. We clean to bare metal along the examination path and avoid shot blasting that could close a crack.

faq.q: Can you examine parts at the turbine site rather than a shop?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope. The site arranges safe access and rescue, and we bring the penetrant system, lighting and cleaning supplies suited to the surface and temperature.
